voice_performance.performance_intent: Someone showing you the working, patiently, because they think you will enjoy the fix. Warmer and slower than the previous production - this is a correction offered, not a measurement reported. No triumph in the voice when the textbook is contradicted.
voice_performance.energy_curve: Even and low on the hook. A small lift on 'it rises again'. The correction is delivered flatly, without relish. Then slows through the three pulls, and the turn is the quietest line in the video.
voice_performance.pause_policy: Two real pauses: one before the correction, one before the turn. Everywhere else the sentence breaks carry it.

provider_notes.piper: Piper has no SSML. The warmth has to come from longer clauses and from length_scale, not from tags; the pauses are real silence placed between per-section renders.

sections.label: Hook
sections.text: There are two high tides a day. Only one of them makes any sense.
sections.speaker_directions: Flat and unhurried. 'Only one' carries the whole hook; do not push it.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: State it like a fact that has been sitting there for years, which it has.

enhancement_cues.description: Warm paper. A coastal section drawn in ink: a strip of shore, the sea, and two horizontal tide marks. The upper mark is labelled once. Construction lines stay visible.

sections.label: The half that makes sense
sections.text: The Moon passes overhead and the sea rises to meet it. Fine. But twelve hours later it rises again, on the side of the planet facing away.
sections.speaker_directions: Even through the first sentence. 'Fine' is dropped in, almost thrown away. Slight lift on 'rises again'.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: 'Fine' should sound like someone conceding the easy half so they can get to the hard one.

enhancement_cues.description: The view pulls back to the whole planet on the plate. The Moon is drawn small at the right margin. The near-side water swells toward it in sea blue. Then, without ceremony, the far side swells too - and the drawing simply sits there being impossible.

sections.label: The wrong answer
sections.text: You were probably taught that centrifugal force flings the far water outward. Physicists call that one a misconception. Nothing out there is being pushed.
sections.speaker_directions: Deliver the correction completely flatly. No relish, no gotcha. A real pause before 'You were probably taught'.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: The viewer learned this in good faith. The line lands harder if the voice is kind about it.

enhancement_cues.description: A curved arrow is drawn onto the plate in vermilion, sweeping outward from the far side, exactly the way a textbook margin would annotate it - and labelled the way a textbook would. Then a single vermilion stroke crosses it out. The struck-through annotation stays on the page; it is not erased.

sections.label: Three pulls
sections.text: Gravity gets weaker with distance. So the Moon pulls the near ocean hardest. It pulls the solid Earth a little less. And the far ocean least of all.
sections.speaker_directions: Slow and even across the three pulls, each one landing as its arrow is drawn. Do not accelerate.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: Three clauses, three arrows. The rhythm of the voice and the rhythm of the drawing must be the same.

enhancement_cues.description: Three vermilion arrows are drawn across the planet on the Moon's axis - near, centre, far - each shorter than the last, each drawn as its clause is spoken. Their lengths are the argument; nothing is labelled.
The three arrows are stacked at the margin against a common baseline so the difference between them is unmistakable.

sections.label: The turn
sections.text: So the planet gets pulled out from under its own water.
sections.speaker_directions: The quietest line in the video. A real pause before it. Let the drawing finish the sentence.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: This is the whole video in one sentence. Do not decorate it.

enhancement_cues.description: The middle arrow - the pull on the Earth itself - is subtracted from all three. What is left points outward at both ends: away from the centre on the near side, and away from the centre on the far side. Two bulges, drawn as arithmetic. This is the hero beat.

sections.label: The check
sections.text: It is also why your bath has no tide. Across a bathtub, that difference is far too small to move anything.
sections.speaker_directions: Lighter, almost an aside. This is the reward for following the argument.

enhancement_cues.description: A bathtub drawn in the same ink on the same plate, with the same three arrows on it - and this time all three are identical. Nothing happens. The still water is the punchline.

sections.label: Landing
sections.text: A tide is not gravity being strong. It is gravity being uneven.
sections.speaker_directions: Even, closing, no lift on the last word.

delivery_cues.delivery_note: No call to action. The reframe is the ending.

enhancement_cues.description: The closing line set in the plate's serif, low on the page, as a caption under a figure.
The plate holds, and the small Moon at the margin keeps drifting slowly outward, still moving as the video ends. It never stops, and it never reaches the edge.

grounding.s3: arXiv 1506.04085 - textbooks introduce a fictitious centrifugal force in a rotating frame, identified as a source of misconception
grounding.s4: NOAA - the Moon's pull varies across the Earth: strongest on the near ocean, weakest on the far
grounding.s5: NOAA / Strassler - the differential force, not rotation, produces both bulges
grounding.s6: NASA - small bodies of water have no tides because the gradient across them is negligible

metadata.timing_note: Measured from the rendered Piper audio (en_US-ryan-high, length_scale 1.12 - slower than the previous production by design). Video runs 46.5s: 0.3s lead-in, 44.87s narration timeline, 1.63s of drift after the last word.
